Introduction

It's best to view this page on a PC screen so you can see the tables properly

Expert Systems are an early form of artificial intelligence designed to simulate the decision making ability of a human expert.

They consist of software packages designed to assist humans in situations where an expert in a specific area of knowledge is required.

This field is based on the notion that humans are still better at various tasks than computer systems.

Some examples of human-optimised vs computer-optimised tasks are listed below:

Human-Optimised Balanced Ability Computer- Optimised
Creativity Complex Motion Information Processing
Emotion / Empathy Vision
Planning / Executive Function Language
Consciousness Structured Problem Solving

Expert systems are designed to encode the knowledge and experience gained by human experts.

Expert Systems Process

  • Obtain the knowledge required from an expert
  • Express the knowledge as a collection of rules in the form of logical implications (knowledge base).
  • Draw conclusions from the knowledge (reasoning).
ChatGPT Expanded

Expert systems are advanced computational models that integrate a substantial amount of specialized knowledge to make decisions or solve problems typically handled by human experts. They are crucial in domains where the expertise is rare, expensive, or requires consistent replication of high-level decision-making. These systems are primarily built on rules that mimic the decision-making process of human experts in specific fields.

System Structure

Expert Systems are comprised of a knowledge base and/or database, which is connected to an inference engine. A user interface is also provided to allow humans to interact with the system's components.

Knowledge Base

The knowledge base will often contain the specific knowledge needed for decision making
This knowledge is structured in the form of rules (depicted as statements)

  • An example could be:
    if: (patient has a sore throat) & (patient has a fever)
    then: (patient may have a cold)

The knowledge base is supplemented by a database containing factual data and relationships about the domain of the problem.

Inference Engine

  • The inference engine represents the core of an expert system.
  • It will compare each rule stored in the knowledge base with factual information contained in the database.
  • Reasoning methodologies are used to arrive at conclusions or solutions. Reasoning can be forward-chaining or backward-chaining (explained later).
  • The inference engine will cycle via a match-fire procedure.

User Interface

The User Interface component allows for interaction between users and the expert system. They are designed to be easy to input data and ask questions.

Concepts

Knowledge Representation

Knowledge can be represented in two possible ways:

  • Procedurally within a programming language
  • Via production rules (if-then expressions)

Antecedents and Consequents
A rule will fire when the condition is satisfied and the action is executed.

    • 'Antecedent' is the technical term for the premise or condition
    • 'Consequent' is the technical term for the conclusion or action

Rules can have multiple antecedents, combined via conjunction (technical term for AND) or disjunction. (technical term for OR).

  • Consequents can also have multiple clauses.

Rule Representation

Rules can be representative of numerous real-life situations.

Definition Example
Relation If X happened, then Y is true If (fuel tank empty), then (car won't start)
Recommendation If X happens, then advice is to do Y If (it is snowing) then (wear a big coat)
Directive If X happened, then instruction is to do Y If (fuel tank empty) then (refuel the car)
Strategies If X, then do action Y.
Step 1 completed.
(Action Y involves checking for circumstance Z)
If Step 1 completed and Z is true, then do action W.
Step 2 completed.
 If (car is dead) then (check fuel tank).
Step 1 complete.
If (fuel tank empty) and (Step 1 complete)
then (check the battery).
Step 2 complete.
Heuristics If X, and Y == (numerical value)
and Z (... etc)
then W has occurred		 If the spill is liquid and the pH > 0 and the smell is vinegar
then the spill is acetic acid.

Inferencing

Inference Chain Example

  • Inference chains will consist of a chain of rules that draw from the given knowledge, which is value-set by the given factual information.
  • This allows for the creation of logical event flows that are influenced by the given data.

Reasoning

Reasoning, as explained above, can be forward-chaining or backward-chaining.

ChatGPT Explanation

Forward Chaining: This data-driven approach starts with the data at hand and applies rules to infer further facts until a conclusion is reached or no more rules apply. It is useful in exploratory analysis or when multiple outcomes or paths need to be explored simultaneously.

Backward Chaining: This goal-driven approach starts with a hypothesis or a conclusion and works backward to find supporting evidence or conditions. It is particularly effective in diagnostic systems where the goal is to validate a specific condition or diagnosis.

Forward-Chaining

  • Forward chaining is a technique whereby information is gathered first, and then inferred upon. It is data-driven and starts with known facts.
  • Forward chaining is useful when we do not only want to infer more than one particular fact, since it is the facts we start with.
  • Many rules may be executed within forward chaining, that have nothing to do with the end result.

Backward-Chaining

  • Backward chaining is a goal-driven technique that involves starting with a goal state and attempting to find evidence to prove it.
  • The knowledge base is searched initially to find rules that may have the desired solution.
  • These rules must have the goal in the block of the logical flow.
  • If a rule of this nature is found, and the condition matches known data in the system, the rule is fired and the goal is provided.
  • It is rare that the inference engine will find this rule on a first attempt, so the rule will usually be put aside and added to a stack, with a subgoal created to prove the given condition.
  • The stacking process is repeated until no rules are found for the current subgoal.

Choice of Reasoning

The forward chain inference engine is chosen in situations where an expert needs to find a goal or solution from existing data.
The backward chain inference engine is chosen in situations where an expert begins with a hypothetical solution or end state and needs to find the facts and/or evidence in the data to prove that state.

Conflict Resolution

Conflicts occur within expert systems where two rules have the same antecedent.
For example, if we have three rules in a simple traffic light system:

  1. IF light is green THEN go
  2. IF light is red THEN stop and check for pedestrians
  3. IF light is green THEN stop and check for pedestrians
  • Since (1) and (3) have the same antecedent (IF part), a conflict is created between them.
  • Inference engines (the forward-chain or backward-chain systems) must determine which rule to fire in these circumstances.
  • This is known as conflict resolution.

Forward Chain Conflict Resolution

  • In forward chaining, both rules will be fired.
  • Rule 1 would be fired first as it is the topmost rule, giving an output value of "go" in our example.
  • Rule 3 would be fired next, giving a final output value of "stop and check..." in the example.

Conflict Resolution Methods
Conflict resolution methods can also be application-defined.

  • Highest Priority: Rule ordering can be used to select the highest priority rule for execution.
  • Highest Specificity: Rules can be giving a specificity ranking, with more general rules placed lower in this ranking. The system can therefore be set to execute the rule that is the most specific.
    • This works on the assumption that specific rules process more data than general ones.
  • Most Recent Data: By attaching time tags to the stored data, the system can be set to fire the rule whereby the antecedent uses the most recent information added to the database.

Metaknowledge and Metarules

Metaknowledge can be understood as 'knowledge about knowledge'. It refers to information about the use and control of the knowledge contained within the expert system.

Metaknowledge is governed by metarules, which can be thought of as 'rules dictating how rules function'. A metarule determines a strategy for the use of task-specific rules within the system.

Some examples of metarules contained within an expert system could be:

  • Rules supplied by experts have higher priorities than rules supplied by novices.
  • Rules governing the rescue of human lives have higher priorities than rules concerned with clearing overloads on power system equipment.
ChatGPT Expanded

Metaknowledge, or knowledge about how knowledge is used, plays a critical role in managing and organizing the knowledge base. Metarules are higher-order rules that govern how other rules are applied, ensuring that the expert system's reasoning aligns with strategic or operational priorities.

Summary

Advantages of Expert/Rule-Based System Use

  • Allow for the representation of knowledge in a natural, human-like way via simplistic logical expressions of IF this THEN that.
  • Allows for a uniform structure among rules, with each rule signifying an independent piece of knowledge.
    • All rules following IF … THEN structure allows for a uniform standard.
  • Allows for the separation of knowledge and knowledge processing steps. This makes it possible to develop different applications that utilise the same expert system shell.
  • Allows for reasoning with incomplete or unknown knowledge. This is useful in situations where a lack of knowledge in a particular area needs to be communicated clearly to the end user.

Disadvantages of Expert/Rule-Based System Use

  • It may be difficult to analyse how well individual rules serve the overall strategy. Logical interactions taking place within large sets of rules may not be as transparent as other AI based systems.
  • Speed: Inference cycles will typically search through all production rules exhaustively. This makes expert systems with large sets of rules slow and they can be unsuitable for real-time use.
  • Inability to learn: Unlike AI based systems such as neural networks, expert systems are not adaptive and cannot modify or adjust their own rules through any kind of learning.

Expert system rules are static and cannot change without human modification, meaning a knowledge engineer is typically required to maintain the system.

Expert systems are also not human-like in the sense that they truly understand the data being fed to them. Human experts, for example, know when to break the rules and will have experience as to situations where rules do not apply as normal.
